newsitem.title: UK: UK input prices to fall again in December.
newsitem.headline: UK input prices to fall again in December.

text.p: UK input prices are expected to have dropped further in December after their sharp dip in November, as the soaring pound continues to slash the cost of imported raw materials, economists said on Friday.
The producer price data, due at 0930 GMT on Monday, will confirm benign pipeline inflationary pressures in the UK, but are unlikely to alleviate pressure for an interest rate rise.
A Reuter poll found economists expect seasonally adjusted input prices to fall by 0.9 percent in December, giving a 6.6 percent decline on the year.
Output prices are seen rising 0.8 percent but that translates into only a 2.0 percent annual inflation rate, down from 2.1 percent in November.

"On the input price side, the rise in sterling will help to offset the rise in oil prices in dollar terms and will make sure non-oil commodity prices should have fallen," said Lehman Brothers economist Michael Dicks, who is forecasting a 0.5 percent fall in input prices on the month.
"Overall costs should be down but it won't be as big a drop as in November." On a trade-weighted basis, sterling has risen by around 14 percent since August last year.
Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets, expected an even more dramatic fall in input prices.
"Our commodity index proved an excellent indicator of the change in unadjusted input prices in November, and in December the index rose by an average of 0.2 percent on November's level," he said.
"We think this points to a 0.8 percent month-on-month fall in seasonally adjusted input prices."
Daiwa economist Katy Peters expected output price inflation to continue falling in the coming months.

She said output prices would be boosted slightly in December by excise duty changes in the Budget. "But they were also boosted this time last year so there'll be no significant impact on the annual rate."

Economists said while the data may give a slight boost to the short end of the gilt yield curve, they would do little to sway expectations of further interest rate rises in either January or February.

"Short sterling will get some boost from the data, but it won't have a significant impact," said Peters. "Part of the problem is that the good PPI data is not feeding through to retail price inflation because margins are being increased."
Economists said Bank of England governor Eddie George would take little comfort from the data when he meets Chancellor of the Exchquer Kenneth Clarke next Wednesday.
According to a Reuter poll, 12 of 20 analysts surveyed believe Clarke will keep rates unchanged after the meeting.
